title: Trump's new tariffs over forced labor are unlikely to survive a court challenge
gist: PIIE's Alan Wm. Wolff argues the Trump administration's newest tariff rationale — alleging inadequate foreign action against forced labor to justify 10-12.5% Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies — is likely to be struck down by the Supreme Court, just as its prior IEEPA and Section 122 tariff justifications were. He contends the tariffs' uniform, undifferentiated design suggests the real purpose is preserving global tariff coverage rather than combating forced labor.

themes.theme: A third tariff rationale, likely to meet the same fate

insights.claim: The Trump administration has cycled through three different legal rationales for near-global tariffs — national emergency powers (IEEPA), a balance-of-payments problem (Section 122), and now inadequate foreign action against forced labor (Section 301) — with the first two struck down or expired and the third predicted to fail as well.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Investors should expect continued legal uncertainty and reversal risk around US comprehensive tariffs regardless of which statutory justification the administration invokes next.
insights.quote: The first two approaches failed to achieve the administration's objective of lasting world-wide US tariffs, and the third will probably fail as well.

insights.claim: The Supreme Court struck down Trump's April 2025 'Liberation Day' IEEPA tariffs in February 2026, and separately the Court of International Trade found the US did not have a balance-of-payments problem under Section 122, causing those 10 percent across-the-board tariffs to expire on July 24, 2026.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Establishes a track record of US courts rejecting broad presidential tariff authority, a precedent relevant to any pending or future litigation over new tariff actions.

insights.claim: The new Section 301(b) forced-labor tariffs (10% or 12.5% on 60 economies) were proposed in June 2026 and are set to begin rolling out the same week the prior Section 122 tariffs expire, suggesting the administration is using forced labor as a new pretext to keep tariff coverage continuous rather than pursuing a distinct labor policy goal.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Tariff exposure for importers of goods from the 60 named economies is likely to persist without interruption even as the legal justification changes, keeping trade-policy risk elevated.

themes.theme: Constitutional and legal vulnerabilities of the forced-labor tariffs

insights.claim: Congress did not delegate, and constitutionally cannot delegate, authority for the president to determine and implement comprehensive tariff policy covering virtually all trading partners, making the forced-labor tariffs another instance of presidential overreach likely to be overturned if challenged in court.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: The core legal thesis for why these tariffs are a poor basis for long-term corporate planning around sourcing and pricing.
insights.locator: The planned tariffs to combat forced labor

insights.claim: Section 301 retaliatory authority requires a finding that a targeted country's acts, policies, or practices burden US commerce; the 60 countries targeted for the forced-labor tariffs account for nearly all US imports and 90 percent of world trade, making it doubtful this burden requirement can be credibly satisfied for such a sweeping group simultaneously.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Gives a specific, checkable legal test — the 'burden on US commerce' finding — that litigation watchers can track as the case for or against these tariffs develops.
insights.locator: That requirement is not clearly satisfied

insights.claim: The Supreme Court's 2024 ruling in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, holding that executive agencies cannot interpret for themselves the extent of their own authority, extends by the author's reasoning to the presidency and undercuts the administration's claim of implicit authority to impose secondary sanctions via Section 301.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific precedent likely to be cited against the administration in court, useful for legal-risk modeling.
insights.locator: The Supreme Court stipulated in Loper Bright

insights.claim: This would be the first-ever use of Section 301 retaliatory authority to impose simultaneous secondary sanctions on multiple countries at once, an application of the statute Congress never contemplated when passing the Trade Act of 1974.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Untested legal theories carry higher reversal risk, reinforcing the case that these tariffs are a fragile basis for durable trade-policy assumptions.
insights.locator: never used before in this manner

insights.claim: The author paraphrases Chief Justice John Roberts to argue that even as circumstances change, the Constitution's allocation of tariff-setting power to Congress does not, framing the setting of broad tariffs as the sole prerogative of Congress rather than the president.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Signals the durability of the constitutional argument beyond this single administration — a structural, not just political, constraint on future tariff actions.
insights.quote: To paraphrase Chief Justice John Roberts Jr., times change, the Constitution does not.

themes.theme: Economic costs and evidence the policy design is pretextual

insights.claim: Research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York finds that American businesses and consumers bear 90 percent of the cost of a comprehensive tariff, meaning the economic burden of the forced-labor tariffs would fall overwhelmingly on the US economy rather than on foreign producers or governments.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
entities: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
insights.so_what: Reinforces that broad tariffs function largely as a domestic tax on US importers and consumers, relevant to inflation and corporate margin forecasting.
insights.quote: Americans, whether businesses or end consumers, bear 90 percent of its cost, according to researchers at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

insights.claim: The 60 targeted economies are sorted into just two categories — those with forced-labor laws and those without — and assigned uniform tariffs of 10 or 12.5 percent regardless of actual differences in each country's conduct or performance, a lack of differentiation the author says suggests the real objective is maintaining global tariff coverage rather than incentivizing better labor practices.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: A crude, binary tariff structure with no gradation is a tell that the labor-rights framing is secondary to revenue/leverage goals, useful for assessing how likely the policy is to be narrowed or negotiated away country-by-country.
insights.quote: The lack of differentiation suggests that the administration's primary objective may be maintaining global tariffs, rather than crafting a carefully calibrated response to the problem of forced labor.
insights.locator: The tariffs' design also raises questions

insights.claim: There is no evidence that changing the stated US rationale for tariffs will materially reduce forced labor in trading-partner countries, since underlying trade relationships and foreign enforcement mechanisms remain unchanged by the relabeling.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Suggests the stated policy goal (reducing forced labor) is unlikely to be achieved even if the tariffs survive, weakening the policy's stated justification for continuity.

themes.theme: Existing US and international frameworks are already bypassed

insights.claim: The United States has already barred imports of goods made with forced labor since 1930, and Section 301 already designates forced labor as an actionable foreign practice, meaning the new tariffs largely duplicate existing legal tools rather than filling a policy gap.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Undercuts the stated necessity of new tariffs, since existing 1930-era import bans and Section 301 already address forced labor directly.
insights.locator: Forced labor is already dealt with under US law

insights.claim: Even the historical US response to apartheid-era South Africa did not rely on secondary sanctions — penalizing one country for its dealings with another — making the proposed forced-labor secondary sanctions against 60 countries an unprecedented escalation in US trade-policy tools.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Historical precedent suggests the scale of the proposed secondary-sanctions approach is a significant departure from past US practice, adding to its legal vulnerability.
insights.locator: Even the US response to apartheid

insights.claim: The US has not ratified either the ILO's 1930 Forced Labor Convention (181 ratifying states) or its 2014 Protocol (61 ratifying countries), which the author suggests may be linked in part to the US practice of subcontracting prison operations to private companies that can profit from forced or prison labor.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Highlights a credibility gap in the US invoking forced labor as a tariff justification while remaining outside the primary international legal framework addressing the issue.
insights.locator: The United States, however, has not ratified

themes.theme: WTO dysfunction and the US role in it

insights.claim: Following the WTO ministerial conference in Cameroon, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer called the WTO 'not a serious forum' for global trade governance, specifically criticizing its handling of seafood commerce and fisheries.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Signals continued US disengagement from multilateral trade governance, relevant to exporters and sectors (like seafood/fisheries) reliant on WTO rules.

insights.claim: The WTO's 166 members rarely reach consensus on binding rules and its dispute-settlement system can no longer issue final determinations — a dysfunction the author says the US itself is currently an important source of, having led efforts to block rule enforcement and sided with members resisting new rules.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: US-driven WTO paralysis means multilateral trade dispute resolution is unlikely to constrain unilateral US tariff actions in the near term.
insights.locator: the United States is currently an important source

insights.claim: WTO rules already permit member countries to act unilaterally against products of prison labor, meaning an existing multilateral legal avenue exists that does not require the administration's new bilateral secondary-tariff approach.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Points to a lower-risk, already-legal alternative path the administration could have used instead of a constitutionally contested one.
insights.locator: leaves countries free to act against the products of prison labor

themes.theme: The path not taken: negotiating an international standard

insights.claim: Given the size of US economic leverage demonstrated under Trump's second term, genuine international negotiation on a forced-labor convention would likely find willing partners — but the administration has not called for such negotiations, which the author reads as evidence its real objective is restoring global tariffs rather than curbing forced labor.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: For investors, this implies the forced-labor rationale is a legally fragile vehicle for a broader tariff strategy, so trade-policy risk should be tracked through litigation outcomes rather than through developments on the labor issue itself.

top_entities: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
